points.question: Does the company have right operational costs? The more durable a competitive advantage, the less a business has to spend to maintain it. If they are building cars or designing software, they may not have to buy big expensive jets, or can use the same equipment for twenty years without any risk of obsolescence. If the answer is yes, be careful.

points.question: What is the initial rate of return on the investment and how does it compare to the return on U.S. treasury bonds? The price you pay to BUY determines your rate of return - pay less, earn more; pay more, earn less. Take the company's current per share earnings and divide it by the current price of a single share. This will give you the investment's initial rate of return. Then compare the investment's initial rate of return and expected growth rate per share to the return being paid on U.S. treasury bonds. If the treasuries look juicier, the stock might be overpriced.

points.title: Projected annual compounding return as an equity/bond (Book Value model)
points.question: What is the company's projected annual compounding return as an equity/bond? paragraphs: Receivables vs. Revenue Growth: Days sales outstanding moved +13 days over 5 years while revenue compounded 23.2%. Receivables are growing faster than sales, which can flatter revenue recognition and must be watched.
